name: In Good Order
verified: 2026-11-08 · read end to end from the published page
intro:
🚫 USE MADE-UP DETAILS. NOTHING REAL. No real bank account, no real account number, no real PIN, no real password, no real M-Pesa details. Not even your own. Invent everything: "Equity, account 1234567890, PIN 4321". Everything this test needs works perfectly well with invented details.

Why we are strict about this: typing your real bank details and your real PIN into an app you have only just met is exactly what a scam looks like, and Daraja Academy's own first lesson teaches older people to refuse it. We are not going to train our own testers to do the thing we teach customers not to do. The app itself is sound — it locks everything with your passphrase and sends nothing anywhere — but the habit matters more than this one app.

⚠️ THIS APP IS NOT FINISHED. Jerry has not decided whether it ever becomes a product. So this is an early test, not a last check before it goes on sale. Anything that confuses you is worth reporting, however small, and "I did not understand what this section was for" is a real finding here.

🔑 ONE MORE THING BEFORE YOU START. This app has no password reset. If you forget the passphrase you choose in step 2, everything inside is gone for good and nobody — not Jerry, not Claude, not anybody — can open it. That is on purpose. Choose something you will remember for the next hour, and write it on paper beside you.

steps.do: This app is not ready to test yet — it has no address a phone can open. If you have reached this step, tell Jerry: nothing should have sent you here.
steps.see: Nothing to see. Stop here and go back to your list.

steps.do: Read the "First time?" note properly, before typing anything. Then, without looking back at it, write down in the box below what you think happens if somebody forgets their passphrase.
steps.see: The note says there is no reset. Your answer is the test here, not the app's: if the note did not make that clear to you, it is not clear enough for a customer either. Say so plainly — that is a real problem, not a complaint.

steps.do: Type a made-up passphrase you will remember for the next hour — a short sentence works, for example "blue gate at mama njeri shop". Write it on paper. Type it again in the second box. Tap "Create the binder".
steps.see: The lock screen goes and you land on a page headed "The binder", with nine squares: Call these people first, Bank & money, Insurance, Bills & subscriptions, Property & vehicles, Accounts & passwords, Medical, Where the papers are, Wishes & letters. Each says "empty".

steps.do: Try a short passphrase first if you like — type something under 8 characters and tap the button before doing step 3 properly.
steps.see: It refuses, and says to use at least 8 characters. If it let a short one through, say so.

steps.do: Read the nine section names and nothing else. Before opening any of them, say which one you would not have thought to include, and whether any are in a strange order to you.
steps.see: There is no right answer here. We want to know whether these nine make sense to a Kenyan family, since they were written for an American one.

steps.do: Tap "Call these people first". Open "+ Add an entry". Put in a made-up person: name "Mwangi the lawyer", details "0700 000 000, Nakuru, did the land papers", notes "he has the title deed". Tap "Save entry".
steps.see: The entry appears in the list, a small message says "Saved & encrypted", and the + section closes ready for another.

steps.do: Go back with "‹ All sections" and tap "Bank & money". Add one made-up account — invent everything: name "Equity, everyday account", details "account 1234567890, Nakuru branch", and in the Password / PIN box type a made-up PIN such as 4321. Save it.
steps.see: This section has a Password / PIN box that the first section did not. The saved entry shows the PIN as dots, with "(tap to show)" beside it.
The made-up PIN appears. Tap it again and it goes back to dots. If it stays visible, say so — that matters on a shared phone.

steps.do: Tap "🔒 Lock" at the top right. Then open the app again and type the WRONG passphrase.
steps.see: It refuses, with words to the effect that the passphrase does not open this binder. It does not say whether the passphrase or the binder is the problem, which is deliberate.

steps.do: Now type your real made-up passphrase from step 3.
steps.see: Both entries are still there, exactly as you left them.

steps.do: Put the phone down and do not touch the screen for five minutes. Make tea. Come back and look.
steps.see: It has locked itself and is asking for the passphrase again. Tell us how that felt: safe, or annoying? Five minutes is the app's choice and we can change it.

steps.do: Unlock it again and tap "🖨 Print the binder". Do not print to a real printer — look at the preview your phone shows, then cancel.
steps.see: ⚠️ READ THIS BEFORE YOU LOOK: the printed page shows the PIN and password in PLAIN TEXT, not dots. That is on purpose — the paper copy is meant for a locked box at home. But it means you must never print this on a shared or office printer. Tell us whether you would have known that without being told. If you would not have, the app needs to say it on the button.
Your phone offers to save a file. Say whether it saved, where it went, and whether you could tell what happened. If nothing seemed to happen at all, that is the finding.

steps.do: Open "Wishes & letters" — the last section. Read the small line under the heading. Add one made-up entry: name "For my children", notes a sentence or two you invent.
steps.see: The app calls this the page that matters most. Does it feel like somewhere a person could actually write something personal, or does it feel like a form? This is the section we most want your honest opinion on.

steps.do: Look at the very bottom of the page, under everything.
steps.see: A line saying the app is by Daraja Studio, that everything stays on the device, and that it is not legal advice. Say whether anything in that line surprises you or sounds untrue after using it.

steps.do: Last. Using it as a whole: would you put your own family's real details in this, once it is finished? Answer honestly — "no" is as useful as "yes", and more useful if you can say why.
steps.see: There is nothing to check on screen. This is the question Jerry is actually asking.

parked: In Good Order has no public address yet — it exists only as a Claude artifact, which a tester cannot open. The script is kept because the 16 steps are good; it cannot be run until the app is published to this repository like every other. Parked 8 Nov 2026. It is on no list, so nobody is blocked by this.
